title: Configure and verify access control lists

questions.question: How are ACL entries processed?
questions.explanation: ACLs are read top-down and stop at the first match.

correct.explanation: ACLs evaluate top-down — first match wins; implicit deny any at the end.

incorrect.explanation: ACLs are not bottom-up — order matters; put specific permits before broad denies.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Bottom-up points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for processing order.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "processing order", Top-down, first match wins satisfies what this question tests — Bottom-up does not.

incorrect.explanation: IOS does not auto-sort by specificity — you must order lines correctly.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Most-specific first automatically points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for processing order.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "processing order", Top-down, first match wins satisfies what this question tests — Most-specific first automatically does not.

incorrect.explanation: Evaluation is deterministic top-down — never random.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Randomly points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for processing order.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "processing order", Top-down, first match wins satisfies what this question tests — Randomly does not.

answerReview.examTip: ACL order trap → first match wins. Place explicit permits before catch-all deny.

questions.question: True or False: An ACL has an implicit deny-all at the end.
questions.explanation: True — anything not explicitly permitted is denied.

correct.explanation: Every Cisco ACL has an implicit deny any at the end — unmatched traffic is dropped.

incorrect.explanation: Without the implicit deny, unmatched traffic would be permitted — IOS denies by default at ACL end.
incorrect.whatItDoes: False states the opposite of the tested fact about implicit deny.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "implicit deny", True satisfies what this question tests — False does not.

answerReview.examTip: No match at bottom of ACL → implicit deny all.

questions.question: Where should a standard ACL be placed?
questions.explanation: Standard ACLs match source only, so place them near the destination to avoid over-blocking.

correct.explanation: Standard ACLs match source IP only — place them close to the destination so you do not accidentally filter traffic for other subnets earlier.

incorrect.explanation: Near the source is correct for extended ACLs (match source and destination) — standard ACLs belong near the destination.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Applying extended ACL placement rule to standard ACL
incorrect.whatItDoes: Close to the source points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for standard placement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "standard placement", Close to the destination satisfies what this question tests — Close to the source does not.

incorrect.explanation: ACLs are applied on specific interfaces where traffic enters or exits — not blindly on every interface.
incorrect.whatItDoes: On every interface points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for standard placement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "standard placement", Close to the destination satisfies what this question tests — On every interface does not.

incorrect.explanation: Trunks carry multiple VLANs — ACL placement follows source/destination logic, not “trunks only”.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Restricting ACL placement to trunk interfaces
incorrect.whatItDoes: Only on trunks expects VLAN tags on a link that should behave as access-only in this stem.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "standard placement", Close to the destination satisfies what this question tests — Only on trunks does not.

answerReview.examTip: Extended ACL → near source. Standard ACL → near destination.

questions.question: Where should an extended ACL be placed?
questions.explanation: Extended ACLs are specific, so place near the source to drop traffic early.

correct.explanation: Place extended ACLs close to the source — filter unwanted traffic before it crosses the network.

incorrect.explanation: Close to destination is the rule for standard ACLs (source-only matching).
incorrect.whatItDoes: Close to the destination points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for extended placement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: The stem asks what gets learned (extended placement). Switches record the source MAC on ingress — destination MAC is for lookup, not learning.

incorrect.explanation: Root bridge is STP terminology — unrelated to ACL placement.
incorrect.whatItDoes: On the root bridge points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for extended placement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "extended placement", Close to the source satisfies what this question tests — On the root bridge does not.

incorrect.explanation: DHCP server placement does not determine extended ACL filter location.
incorrect.whatItDoes: On the DHCP server points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for extended placement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "extended placement", Close to the source satisfies what this question tests — On the DHCP server does not.

answerReview.examTip: Extended ACL → near source; standard ACL → near destination.

questions.question: What wildcard mask matches exactly the /24 network 192.168.1.0?

correct.explanation: For 192.168.1.0/24, wildcard 0.0.0.255 matches the entire /24 (care bits on last octet only).

incorrect.explanation: 255.255.255.0 is a subnet mask, not the wildcard for a /24 host match.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 255.255.255.0 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for wildcard mask.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "wildcard mask", 0.0.0.255 satisfies what this question tests — 255.255.255.0 does not.

incorrect.explanation: 0.0.0.0 matches one host only — not the full /24.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 0.0.0.0 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for wildcard mask.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "wildcard mask", 0.0.0.255 satisfies what this question tests — 0.0.0.0 does not.

incorrect.explanation: 255.255.255.255 matches any address — too broad for exactly one /24.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 255.255.255.255 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for wildcard mask.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "wildcard mask", 0.0.0.255 satisfies what this question tests — 255.255.255.255 does not.

answerReview.examTip: /24 ACL wildcard = 0.0.0.255 (invert the mask).

questions.question: Which number range is a standard ACL?

correct.explanation: Standard ACL numbers are 1–99 (and extended 100–199) on CCNA — standard matches source IP only.

incorrect.explanation: 100–199 is the classic range for extended ACLs.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 100–199 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for standard range.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "standard range", 1–99 satisfies what this question tests — 100–199 does not.

incorrect.explanation: 200–299 is not the primary CCNA standard ACL range.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 200–299 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for standard range.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "standard range", 1–99 satisfies what this question tests — 200–299 does not.

incorrect.explanation: 1300–2699 are expanded ACL numbers — standard is 1–99.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 1300–2699 only points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for standard range.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "standard range", 1–99 satisfies what this question tests — 1300–2699 only does not.

answerReview.examTip: Standard ACL = 1–99; extended = 100–199.

questions.question: What can an extended ACL match that a standard ACL cannot?
questions.explanation: Extended ACLs match source+destination IP, protocol, and ports.

correct.explanation: Extended ACLs match source/destination IP, protocol, and port — standard ACLs match source IP only.

incorrect.explanation: Standard ACLs can match source IP — extended adds destination, protocol, and ports.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Source IP points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for extended match.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "extended match", Destination IP, protocol, and port satisfies what this question tests — Source IP does not.

incorrect.explanation: ACLs filter traffic — they are not applied by interface name in the ACE itself.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Interface name points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for extended match.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "extended match", Destination IP, protocol, and port satisfies what this question tests — Interface name does not.

incorrect.explanation: VLAN filtering uses different mechanisms — extended ACLs match L3/L4 fields.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: VLAN ID in standard vs extended
incorrect.whatItDoes: VLAN ID points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for extended match.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "extended match", Destination IP, protocol, and port satisfies what this question tests — VLAN ID does not.

answerReview.examTip: Need port/protocol filter → extended ACL.

questions.question: Which command applies ACL 100 inbound on an interface?
questions.explanation: ip access-group 100 in applies the ACL to the interface.

correct.explanation: Apply with ip access-group 100 in (or out) under interface configuration.

incorrect.explanation: access-list 100 in is not valid interface syntax — use ip access-group.
incorrect.whatItDoes: access-list 100 in applies an ACL type (standard vs extended) or number range that may not match placement rules here.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: ACL placement/match (apply acl): ip access-group 100 in uses the right ACL type and position — access-list 100 in mismatches standard vs extended rules.

incorrect.explanation: ip access-list defines/edits the ACL — ip access-group applies it.
incorrect.whatItDoes: ip access-list 100 inbound applies an ACL type (standard vs extended) or number range that may not match placement rules here.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: ACL placement/match (apply acl): ip access-group 100 in uses the right ACL type and position — ip access-list 100 inbound mismatches standard vs extended rules.

incorrect.explanation: apply acl is not Cisco IOS syntax.
incorrect.whatItDoes: apply acl 100 in points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for apply acl.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "apply acl", ip access-group 100 in satisfies what this question tests — apply acl 100 in does not.

answerReview.examTip: Apply ACL on interface → ip access-group <num> in|out.

questions.question: A specific `deny` never takes effect because a broad `permit` sits above it. Why?
choices: First match wins — the permit matches first
questions.explanation: Top-down first-match means the earlier broad permit matches before the specific deny.

correct.explanation: ACLs use first match wins — a broad permit above a specific deny never reaches the deny line.

incorrect.explanation: Deny rules work — order determines which ACE matches first.
incorrect.whatItDoes: ACLs ignore deny rules points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for order matters.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "order matters", First match wins — the permit matches first satisfies what this question tests — ACLs ignore deny rules does not.

incorrect.explanation: Wildcard masks define match scope — order still governs which ACE hits.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Deny rules need a wildcard points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for order matters.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "order matters", First match wins — the permit matches first satisfies what this question tests — Deny rules need a wildcard does not.

incorrect.explanation: An unapplied ACL filters nothing — here the permit matches before deny due to order.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Unapplied ACL as reason deny fails
incorrect.whatItDoes: The ACL is not applied points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for order matters.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "order matters", First match wins — the permit matches first satisfies what this question tests — The ACL is not applied does not.

answerReview.examTip: Put specific denies before broad permits — first match wins.

questions.question: Identify the range of a standard access list?

correct.explanation: Standard numbered ACLs use range 1–99 (and 1300–1999 extended standard on some platforms) — classic CCNA answer is 1–99.

incorrect.explanation: 100 is not in the standard ACL range — standard stops at 99 in the classic numbering scheme.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 1 to 100 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", 1 to 99 satisfies what this question tests — 1 to 100 does not.

incorrect.explanation: 100–199 is the extended ACL numbered range — not standard.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 100 to 199 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", 1 to 99 satisfies what this question tests — 100 to 199 does not.

incorrect.explanation: 200 is outside both classic standard and extended ranges — standard is 1–99.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 100 to 200 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", 1 to 99 satisfies what this question tests — 100 to 200 does not.

answerReview.examTip: Standard ACL 1–99. Extended ACL 100–199. Match range to ACL type.

questions.question: Which statement is correct about a standard ACL?
choices: Conditions can be based upon only the destination address.
Conditions can be based upon only the source address and source port.
Conditions can be based upon only the source address.
Conditions can be based upon the source or destination address and source or destination port.

correct.explanation: Standard ACLs (1–99, 1300–1999) match source IP only — no destination or L4 ports.

incorrect.explanation: Standard ACLs cannot match destination — that's extended ACL territory.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Conditions can be based upon only the destination address. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: The stem asks what gets learned (statement). Switches record the source MAC on ingress — destination MAC is for lookup, not learning.

incorrect.explanation: Standard ACLs match source IP only — no source port (extended ACL feature).
incorrect.whatItDoes: Conditions can be based upon only the source address and source port. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", Conditions can be based upon only the source address. satisfies what this question tests — Conditions can be based upon only the source address and source port. does not.

incorrect.explanation: Matching ports and destination requires an extended ACL (100–199, 2000–2699).
incorrect.whatItDoes: Conditions can be based upon the source or destination address and source or destination port. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: CAM learning stores one mapping per arrival (statement): Conditions can be based upon only the source address. — not both addresses as table entries.

answerReview.examTip: Standard = source only | Extended = src/dst IP + protocol + ports — place standard ACLs close to destination.

questions.question: Identify the range of an extended access list?

correct.explanation: Extended ACLs use numbered range 100–199 — they match source/destination, protocol, and ports.

incorrect.explanation: 1–99 is the standard ACL range (source IP only) — extended lists start at 100.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 1 to 99 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", 100 to 199 satisfies what this question tests — 1 to 99 does not.

incorrect.explanation: ACL ranges are not 1–100 — extended ACLs are 100–199.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 1 to 100 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", 100 to 199 satisfies what this question tests — 1 to 100 does not.

incorrect.explanation: 100–200 is wrong — the extended numbered range ends at 199.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 100 to 200 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", 100 to 199 satisfies what this question tests — 100 to 200 does not.

answerReview.examTip: Numbered ACLs: 1–99/1300–1999 standard; 100–199/2000–2699 extended.

questions.question: Identify at the end of every ACL?

correct.explanation: Every ACL ends with an implicit deny any any — unmatched traffic is dropped (not permitted).

incorrect.explanation: permit any any is not implicit — only deny any any is hidden at the end.
incorrect.whatItDoes: permit any any points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: ACL syntax (identify): deny any any matches the required match fields — permit any any uses the wrong wildcard or match scope.

incorrect.explanation: Logging is optional per ACE — not an automatic ACL footer.
incorrect.whatItDoes: log all points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", deny any any satisfies what this question tests — log all does not.

incorrect.explanation: No marker exists — IOS silently applies implicit deny.
incorrect.whatItDoes: End of ACL marker points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", deny any any satisfies what this question tests — End of ACL marker does not.

answerReview.examTip: Always add explicit permit for needed traffic — implicit deny drops everything else.

questions.question: Which statement is correct about an ACL?
choices: Packets are compared sequentially against each line in an access list, and the last matching condition is the action taken.
Packets are compared sequentially against each line in an access list until a match is made.
Packets are compared, and if no matching rule exists, they are allowed.
At the end of the ACL, there is an implicit allow.

correct.explanation: ACL evaluation is top-down, first match wins — processing stops at the first matching ACE.

incorrect.explanation: The first match decides — not the last matching line.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Packets are compared sequentially against each line in an access list, and the last matching condition is the action taken. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", Packets are compared sequentially against each line in an access list until a match is made. satisfies what this question tests — Packets are compared sequentially against each line in an access list, and the last matching condition is the action taken. does not.

incorrect.explanation: Unmatched packets hit implicit deny — they are not allowed by default.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Packets are compared, and if no matching rule exists, they are allowed. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", Packets are compared sequentially against each line in an access list until a match is made. satisfies what this question tests — Packets are compared, and if no matching rule exists, they are allowed. does not.

incorrect.explanation: There is an implicit deny, not an implicit allow.
incorrect.whatItDoes: At the end of the ACL, there is an implicit allow. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", Packets are compared sequentially against each line in an access list until a match is made. satisfies what this question tests — At the end of the ACL, there is an implicit allow. does not.

answerReview.examTip: Order matters: place specific permits before broad denies — first hit sticks.

questions.question: Identify an advantage of using a standard ACL?

correct.explanation: Standard ACLs match fewer fields → less CPU processing per packet than extended ACLs.

incorrect.explanation: Extended ACLs are more granular/secure for filtering — standard trades specificity for speed.
incorrect.whatItDoes: More secure points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", Less processing overhead satisfies what this question tests — More secure does not.

incorrect.explanation: Specific rules (ports, protocols) need extended ACLs — not standard.
incorrect.whatItDoes: More specific rules points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", Less processing overhead satisfies what this question tests — More specific rules does not.

incorrect.explanation: Blocking applications requires extended ACLs with port/protocol matches.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Blocking of applications points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", Less processing overhead satisfies what this question tests — Blocking of applications does not.

answerReview.examTip: Standard ACL = fast, coarse (source IP) | Extended = slower, precise — place standard near destination.

questions.question: Identify the expanded range of a standard access list?

correct.explanation: Expanded standard ACL range is 1300–1999 — classic range is 1–99.

incorrect.explanation: 1000–1999 is not the standard/expanded split — expanded standard is 1300–1999.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 1000 to 1999 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", 1300 to 1999 satisfies what this question tests — 1000 to 1999 does not.

incorrect.explanation: 1100–1299 is not a valid Cisco ACL range.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 1100 to 1299 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", 1300 to 1999 satisfies what this question tests — 1100 to 1299 does not.

incorrect.explanation: 2000–2699 is the expanded extended ACL range — not standard.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 2000 to 2699 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", 1300 to 1999 satisfies what this question tests — 2000 to 2699 does not.

answerReview.examTip: ACL numbers: 1–99 / 1300–1999 standard | 100–199 / 2000–2699 extended.

questions.question: You need to filter traffic for the 172.16.0.0/12 network. Which wildcard mask would you use?

correct.explanation: /12 on 172.16.0.0 → wildcard 0.15.255.255 (0=must match, 1=don't care).

incorrect.explanation: 255.240.0.0 is a subnet mask — ACL fields need wildcard, not mask.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 255.240.0.0 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for wildcard.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "wildcard", 0.15.255.255 satisfies what this question tests — 255.240.0.0 does not.

incorrect.explanation: 0.0.240.255 does not align to a /12 boundary — recalc from prefix length.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 0.0.240.255 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for wildcard.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "wildcard", 0.15.255.255 satisfies what this question tests — 0.0.240.255 does not.

incorrect.explanation: 255.3.0.0 is not the inverse of /12 — use 0.15.255.255.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 255.3.0.0 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for wildcard.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "wildcard", 0.15.255.255 satisfies what this question tests — 255.3.0.0 does not.

answerReview.examTip: Wildcard = inverse of mask. /12 → 0.15.255.255 for 172.16.0.0/12.

questions.question: Which command would configure an ACL to block traffic coming from 192.168.1.0/24?

correct.explanation: ip access-list 20 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 begins a standard ACL (1–99) blocking source 192.168.1.0/24 with wildcard 0.0.0.255.

incorrect.explanation: ip access-list 100 starts an extended ACL — source-only filter needs standard range 1–99.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Router(config)#ip access-list 100 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 applies an ACL type (standard vs extended) or number range that may not match placement rules here.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: ACL placement/match (configure): Router(config)#ip access-list 20 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 uses the right ACL type and position — Router(config)#ip access-list 100 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 mismatches standard vs extended rules.

incorrect.explanation: CIDR /24 is not valid in IOS ACL lines — use address + wildcard mask.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Router(config)#ip access-list 1 192.168.1.0/24 applies an ACL type (standard vs extended) or number range that may not match placement rules here.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: ACL placement/match (configure): Router(config)#ip access-list 20 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 uses the right ACL type and position — Router(config)#ip access-list 1 192.168.1.0/24 mismatches standard vs extended rules.

incorrect.explanation: Wildcard 255.255.255.0 is inverted — /24 uses 0.0.0.255.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Router(config)#ip access-list 2 192.168.1.0 255.255.255.0 applies an ACL type (standard vs extended) or number range that may not match placement rules here.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: ACL placement/match (configure): Router(config)#ip access-list 20 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 uses the right ACL type and position — Router(config)#ip access-list 2 192.168.1.0 255.255.255.0 mismatches standard vs extended rules.

answerReview.examTip: ACL placement: standard → near destination | extended → near source | wildcard = inverse of subnet mask.

questions.question: If you configure a rule with the address of 0.0.0.0 and wildcard mask of 255.255.255.255, what are you doing?

correct.explanation: 0.0.0.0 with wildcard 255.255.255.255 matches any address — the 'any' keyword equivalent.

incorrect.explanation: Broadcast is a specific address, not 0.0.0.0/255.255.255.255 match-all.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Defining the broadcast address describes flooding the frame to multiple ports in the VLAN.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "you configure a rule with the address of 0", Defining all addresses satisfies what this question tests — Defining the broadcast address does not.

incorrect.explanation: 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255 matches every host — it does not match nothing.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Defining no addresses points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for you configure a rule with the address of 0.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "you configure a rule with the address of 0", Defining all addresses satisfies what this question tests — Defining no addresses does not.

incorrect.explanation: Network address uses host bits 0 with subnet wildcard — not all-ones wildcard.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Defining the network address points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for you configure a rule with the address of 0.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "you configure a rule with the address of 0", Defining all addresses satisfies what this question tests — Defining the network address does not.

answerReview.examTip: ACL placement: standard → near destination | extended → near source | wildcard = inverse of subnet mask.

questions.question: Which statement is correct about applying ACLs to an interface?
choices: An ACL can be applied in only one direction.
An ACL can be applied only to a single protocol.
An ACL can be applied only to a single port.

correct.explanation: IOS ACL interface limits: one direction, one protocol per application, one ACL per direction — all listed are true.

incorrect.explanation: You can apply in and out on the same interface — but only one ACL per direction.
incorrect.whatItDoes: An ACL can be applied in only one direction. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", All of the above. satisfies what this question tests — An ACL can be applied in only one direction. does not.

incorrect.explanation: ACLs can filter ip, tcp, etc. — but each application binds one ACL per direction/protocol context.
incorrect.whatItDoes: An ACL can be applied only to a single protocol. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", All of the above. satisfies what this question tests — An ACL can be applied only to a single protocol. does not.

incorrect.explanation: Multiple ACLs cannot stack on the same interface/direction — all restrictions apply.
incorrect.whatItDoes: An ACL can be applied only to a single port. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", All of the above. satisfies what this question tests — An ACL can be applied only to a single port. does not.

answerReview.examTip: ACL placement: standard → near destination | extended → near source | wildcard = inverse of subnet mask.

questions.question: You need to filter an application. Which type of access list will you use to complete the task?

correct.explanation: Extended ACLs filter by protocol and port — required to block or permit a specific application like HTTP or SSH.

incorrect.explanation: Standard ACLs match source IP only — they cannot filter by TCP/UDP port or application.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Standard points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for application.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "application", Extended satisfies what this question tests — Standard does not.

incorrect.explanation: Dynamic ACLs use reflexive/temporary permits after auth — the stem asks for application filtering, which is extended.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Dynamic ACL for static app filter
incorrect.whatItDoes: Dynamic points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for application.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "application", Extended satisfies what this question tests — Dynamic does not.

incorrect.explanation: Expanded is not an IOS ACL type — use extended ACLs for protocol/port matching.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Expanded as ACL type for applications
incorrect.whatItDoes: Expanded points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for application.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "application", Extended satisfies what this question tests — Expanded does not.

answerReview.examTip: Filter by port/protocol → extended ACL; source IP only → standard.

questions.question: Identify the expanded range of an extended access list?
